괜찮다.gloss: to be fine; to be okay

meanings.en: to be fine; to be okay; to be alright
meanings.note: Used to reassure someone, decline an offer politely, or say something is acceptable.

examples.trans: I'm really fine.
Is it okay if we meet tomorrow?

meanings.note: Refers to the immediate past.

examples.trans: I arrived just now.
What did you just say?

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (noun).

examples.text: 자막은 신디가 손수 친 첫 야외 취침 텐트, 핑크로 해주시면 되고요.
examples.trans: For the caption, you can make it "Cindy's first hand-pitched outdoor tent" in pink.
Here the word for 'as for the caption' is key.

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (noun).

examples.trans: Looks good, right? That caption just now was pretty clever, was it not?
Here the word for 'wit, flair' is key.

있다.gloss: to exist, to have, to stay

meanings.en: to exist, to be (in a place)
meanings.note: Opposite of 없다.
Marks the possessed item with 이/가.

examples.trans: Do you have time?
Nobody is at home.

related.gloss: to not exist, to not have

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (noun).

examples.text: 시간 왜 이렇게 빨리 가, 화면 밋밋해서 죽겠는데!
examples.trans: Why is time flying so fast when the footage is so bland it is killing me!
Here the word for 'screen, footage' is key.

meanings.en: to appear, be published, be achieved (a score/result)
meanings.note: Used for ratings, test scores, or results coming out

examples.trans: I came outside from the house.
The exam results came out well.

meanings.note: Bound noun often contracted to 거 in everyday speech.

examples.trans: This is my bag.
Because I think I'm late.
The weather is bad.
I feel bad.

않다.gloss: to not do, to not be

meanings.en: to not do, to not be
meanings.note: Auxiliary negative verb/adjective used after -지 (long-form negation)

examples.trans: The weather isn't cold today.
I didn't say anything.

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (noun).

examples.text: 백승찬 화면에 나오는 거 나쁘지 않다, 제법이야.
examples.trans: Baek Seung-chan appearing on screen is not bad at all—he actually holds his own.
Here the word for 'is quite impressive' is key.

meanings.note: Plain first-person singular pronoun used with friends, younger people, or subordinates; contracts to 난 with -는 and becomes 내가 before -가.

examples.trans: I'm going to stay home today.
I'll go first.
Did you hear about this editing?
I was busy today because of editing.

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (noun).

examples.text: 내가 편집을 기가 막히게 해서 그렇지, 쟤가 무슨 남자야, 애지!
examples.trans: Only because my editing is phenomenal—what kind of grown man is he, he is just a kid!
Here the word for 'breath, spirit' is key.

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (verb).

examples.text: 내가 편집을 기가 막히게 해서 그렇지, 쟤가 무슨 남자야, 애지!
examples.trans: Only because my editing is phenomenal—what kind of grown man is he, he is just a kid!
This expression comes from 'breathtakingly, brilliantly'.

meanings.en: to do, to perform, to hold
meanings.note: Core verb; also combines with nouns to form verbs.

examples.trans: What are you doing right now?
We are holding a meeting today.

그렇다.gloss: to be so, to do so

meanings.en: to be like that, to be so
meanings.note: ㅎ-irregular; also used as a pro-verb ('do so / say so')

examples.trans: Is that really so?
Don't keep acting like that.

examples.text: 그냥 내버려 둬, 쟤 완전 취했어.
examples.trans: Just leave him alone, he is completely wasted.
The topic of that guy/girl came up during this shoot.

meanings.note: Placed directly before a noun in questions

examples.trans: What kind of music are you listening to right now?
Is something the matter?
Did you hear about this man?
I was busy today because of man.

meanings.note: Contraction of 아이.
Colloquially used to refer to people of the same age or younger.

examples.trans: Kids are running around and playing in the park.
That person has a really good personality.

meanings.note: Casual exclamation used to call someone younger or a close friend.

examples.trans: Hey, come quickly!
Hey, where are you going?

meanings.note: Colloquial contraction of 그런데; introduces a contrast or obstacle.
Used to shift the topic in conversation.

examples.trans: By the way, what time is it now?
I want to go. But I don't have time.

맞다.gloss: to be right, to be correct

meanings.note: Used to confirm facts or answers.

meanings.en: to fit, to suit, to match
meanings.note: E.g., 사이즈가 맞다 ('the size fits').

examples.trans: Yes, that's my phone number.
These shoes fit my feet perfectly.

meanings.note: Negative copula used with nouns (often with -이/가)

examples.trans: It is not my fault.
Today is not Sunday, it's Monday.
How did you get here?
How should we solve this problem?

meanings.note: Takes a complement marked with 이/가.

examples.trans: I want to become a doctor.
It has already become 12 o'clock.

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (adv).

examples.text: 자꾸 잘못 읽으니까 그렇지, 읽지 마!
examples.trans: That is because you keep reading it wrong—do not read between the lines!
Here the word for 'wrongly' is key.

나가다.gloss: to go out, to step outside

meanings.en: to go out, to step outside, to leave a room
meanings.note: 나- ('out') + 가다 ('to go')

examples.trans: Let's step outside for a moment and talk.
He went out of the conference room.
What time is it now?
I'll leave right now.

meanings.note: interrogative pronoun; becomes 누가 before subject particle -가
indefinite pronoun

examples.trans: Did someone come outside?
Who is that person?

meanings.note: Irregular ㅡ-stem verb: 쓰다 + -어 becomes 써.
Commonly used for tools, money, or time.

examples.trans: I write in my diary every night.
I wrote my name on the very first page of the book.

meanings.note: Standard polite affirmative response; also used to acknowledge that one is listening.

examples.trans: Ah, yes.
Yes, I understand.

examples.text: 아줌마, 성빈장은 저 앞에 중국집 이름이에요. 준모가 거기 좋아해요.
examples.trans: Ma'am, that name on his card bill is the Chinese restaurant out front. Joon-mo loves it.

examples.text: 역시 아줌마는 사람 속 뒤집어 놓으시는 게 프로야.
examples.trans: As expected, she is a total pro at turning a person's stomach upside down.

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (verb).

examples.trans: Yes, ma'am, I am free to talk—please go ahead.
This expression comes from 'please speak'.

meanings.note: Used in 선을 긋다 (to draw the line / set boundaries)

examples.trans: Please do not step outside the line.
I drew a line between work and private life.

보다.gloss: to see, to watch; to take (an exam)

meanings.en: to see, to look at, to watch
meanings.note: Primary meaning.
Idiomatic in 시험을 보다.

examples.trans: I watched a movie on the weekend.
I took the driver's license exam.

meanings.note: refers to something known to both speakers or near the listener

examples.trans: That movie was really fun.
What is that person's name?
Did you hear about this female?
I was busy today because of female.

examples.text: 선? 검사? 설마 검사가 예쁘기까지 하겠어?
examples.trans: A blind date? A prosecutor? Could a prosecutor really be pretty too?
The topic of prosecutor came up during this shoot.

meanings.note: Exclamation of surprise or realization.

examples.trans: Oh my, so nice to meet you!
Oh my, I left my phone behind.

meanings.note: Short-form negation placed directly before verbs and adjectives

examples.trans: I'm not going to the office today.
I haven't watched that movie yet.

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (noun).

examples.text: 여기가 바로 편집실이다, 앞으로 네가 가장 많은 밤을 새우게 될 곳이지.
examples.trans: This right here is the editing room—the place where you will pull the most all-nighters from now on.
Here the word for 'is the editing room' is key.

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (verb).

examples.trans: Oh my, he skipped it because he fell asleep in the editing room?
This expression comes from 'because he fell asleep?'.

meanings.note: Emphasizes a change of state or that a new moment has arrived (contrasting with 지금 'right this second').

examples.trans: I have to go home now.
The performance is starting very soon now.

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (noun).

examples.text: 이제 준모도 나이를 먹을 만큼 먹었고 스스로 결정하게 해주시는 게 어떨까요.
examples.trans: Joon-mo is old enough now, so maybe it would be best to let him decide for himself.
Here the word for 'age' is key.

meanings.note: Everyday verb for eating a meal or food; honorific equivalent is 드시다.

examples.trans: Let's eat lunch together.
Did you eat breakfast?
Eat as much as you want.
Results will come out as much as you've tried.

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (adv).

examples.text: 이제 준모도 나이를 먹을 만큼 먹었고 스스로 결정하게 해주시는 게 어떨까요.
examples.trans: Joon-mo is old enough now, so maybe it would be best to let him decide for himself.
Here the word for 'by himself' is key.

meanings.note: verb to decide

examples.trans: I decided.
Let's decide.

meanings.note: Compound of 하다 (to do) and 주다 (to give).

examples.trans: Please help me (do helping for me).
Please do this for me.

meanings.en: to be how, to be in what state
meanings.note: Its adverbial form 어떻게 ('how') is used to ask how something is done or how things turned out.

examples.trans: How do you feel today?
How did the meeting turn out?

examples.text: 아줌마가 여의도 아파트로 쳐들어가신다고요? 아뇨, 제가 얘기하겠습니다!
examples.trans: You will storm into his Yeouido apartment and move in? No, I will talk to him right away!
into the apartment in everyday conversation

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (verb).

examples.text: 아줌마가 여의도 아파트로 쳐들어가신다고요? 아뇨, 제가 얘기하겠습니다!
examples.trans: You will storm into his Yeouido apartment and move in? No, I will talk to him right away!
This expression comes from 'you will barge in?'.
Oh no, please don't feel hurt.
The topic of no (polite) came up during this shoot.

meanings.note: Humble first-person singular pronoun used in polite speech.

examples.trans: I have an induction ceremony.
Follow me.

meanings.note: Contracted form of 이야기하다

examples.trans: Let's talk again later.
Please tell me honestly.

meanings.note: A polite, enthusiastic expression of agreement.

examples.trans: Are you going? Of course!
Of course, no problem.

meanings.note: Combines with 하다 in 말하다 (to speak, to say).

examples.trans: I don't know what you mean.
You speak Korean well.
Listen closely to what I explain.
I eat Korean food well.

meanings.note: verb listen

examples.trans: Listen well.
Listen to a song.

meanings.note: Used in standard farewells 안녕히 계세요 and 안녕히 가세요.

examples.trans: Goodbye! (to someone staying)
Goodbye! (to someone leaving)

meanings.note: Honorific equivalent of 있다; used in 안녕히 계세요 ('goodbye' to someone staying).

examples.trans: Goodbye! (to someone staying)
Is the teacher inside right now?
